utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis. I'm assisted again today by our intern Lisa Hartog and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President; good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and the registrar, who is back with us today. We'll continue with the examination of our witness. Could the usher please bring the witness into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. I hope that you're receiving the interpretation of what is being said. There seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Cuskic.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony yesterday you spoke about the formation of the El Mujahed detachment. It was in August 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you expressed a position of yours. You said that this was probably an attempt to ensure that these foreigners, the Mujahedin, be placed under the control of the ABiH in a certain manner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, but do correct me if I'm wrong, yesterday you said that if they were in ABiH units, if they had been in ABiH units and if they had been under the control of the ABiH, it wouldn't have been necessary to form that detachment.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear; when brigades was formed and when the corps was formed in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, apart from the Territorial Defence staffs and brigades that were part of the army, there were these groups of Mujahedin, and perhaps there were some MOS groups that had remained. They amassed in those remote villages and they were present in certain camps but they weren't members of army units of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, with regard to these Mujahedin, this is a problem that should have been dealt with at a high level, at the level of the supreme command or at a political level. A corps commander couldn't make any decisions about these matters, and especially not a brigade commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the order to form the 3rd Corps command and the commands of subordinate units, I was able to see who was part of those units, and it was clear that they weren't becoming a part of any units and, in the territorial sense, they didn't belong to anyone. They weren't from that area and no one was responsible for them. This was a specific group, and they had not previously been linked to the Territorial Defence. No one had the authority to make them members of other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me. This question, this problem should have been solved at a higher level, at a political level, perhaps. The corps commander and the brigade commander didn't have such responsibility.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the corps commander didn't have such responsibility and this was especially the case for a brigade commander. This is my assessment. I can't say for sure who was responsible, but this was a political issue alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now go back to your testimony when you spoke about army units which existed in Travnik at the time. You also said that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was in Travnik, and their base was there. That was their base in the Medresa, in the school, where the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On page 33, I think you said that members of your brigade had a line of responsibility or held a line facing the Serbian aggressor in the Bijelo Bucje sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you provide us with a brief description of the location of Bijelo Bucje.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. I think it's to the north-west -- I'm sorry, to the south-west of Travnik. If you look from Turbe, perhaps it's four or five kilometres away, towards Mradinska [phoen], Kamenjas, which is a Bosnian village close to the line. And after a certain period of time, the 3rd Battalion took a position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cuskic, do you know that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade had a zone of responsibility in that area towards Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijelo Bucje there were about 30 troops, 30 soldiers from the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and if I remember this well, after the 3rd Battalion went into the field, they were subordinated to the 3rd Battalion. And the -- in the base of the battalion in Travnik, they had general reserve forces, about 70 people, 70 men, perhaps, in the town of Travnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said, I think it was on page 31, that one of the elevations around Travnik which was under the control of the HVO, was Hajdarove Njive.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the elevated positions, and unfortunately, the HVO, in April, already held a lot of those elevated positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Hajdarove Njive exactly?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hajdarove Njive, if you're looking from the exit of Travnik towards Zenica, if you're looking in the direction of Zenica, it's to the north. It's a plateau. It's perhaps 800 metres above sea level and it dominates the entrance to Travnik. When coming from Vitez and Zenica, it's possible to control the Plava Voda feature and the Medresa feature from that position, and the HVO, in addition to 82-millimetre mortar and the Praga, which often opened fire and wounded soldiers and civilians in the town -- well, they had this Praga too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's very near to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Near the entrance to Travnik. As you probably know, Travnik is -- well, not in a canyon, but in a valley between the mountains of Vilenica and the mountain of Bukovice. It's more or less hidden in that valley. And Hajdarove Njive is to the east. It's one gate, one entrance to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, could the witness be shown document P465. We have a sufficient number of copies for everyone. Could the usher please distribute this document to the witness and to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I just have one question for you before you have a look at this document. The 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was part of the Bosanska Krajina ogee; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st battalion of the 7th Brigade was part of the Bosnian Krajina OG; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes:

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an original document. It's a handwritten document from the commander of the OG, Mr. Alagic. He drafted this document himself, and it was later processed in the communications centre and forwarded to the command of the 3rd Corps. This was on the 8th of June, 1993. You can see what the situation is at the lines toward the Chetniks. You can see what action was taken towards the HVO. You can see what action our forces took, and you can see that the 1st Battalion was engaged on the Hajdarove Njive feature, at the Hajdarove Njive feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is General Alagic's handwriting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This report was for the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This is his handwriting, and this was then processed in the communications centre and then sent to Zenica by packet communications. You can see at the bottom it says "Aga," so this means Alagic, and the entirely document was handwritten by him. The situation was a particular one at the time. I have already said that Commander Alagic didn't have full staff in the command. He had to rely on the command of the 17th and about the 8th of June, because of the problems in the zone, he started bringing the command and OG up to strength with the necessary staff. He would sometimes personally draft reports which would then be technically processed, and forwarded to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that this was drafted at 1900 hours. This report should be a report on the combat operations in the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the day on the 8th of June. And you can see for yourself, the heading says the 8th of June, 1993, at 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: General Alagic drafted this report on the basis of the information he had received from the field, and on the basis of the information he had about combat operations in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely on the basis of reports from his subordinates and on the basis of what he himself had seen. I think that on the 8th of June, Commander Alagic managed to withdraw to the village of Krpeljici, if I remember this correctly, and there he established contact with certain forces in the field and gradually set up a forward command post for the OG and a communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 2, it mentions the activities of your brigade. This report describes the situation on that day and it describes the action taken by the 17th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. You can see what I already mentioned, part of my unit managed to take lines that the HVO was going to hand over to the Chetniks. I'm referring to Veliki Kik and Mali Kik. The line was linked up. We joined up with Slimena, and fighting was going on for the transmitter in Vilenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade took action at the Hajdarove Njive feature?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that they were continuing to take action there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the other page, on the second page, under 3, it says that on that day, the 306th Brigade was the only unit that was engaged in military operations. That's under number 3.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This had to do with linking up forces, in fact, and taking over the lines that had been reached, fortifying, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cuskic, such a report reflected the events that took place on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a reliable report. It's an official report for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now turn to the Prosecution, who may start with their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I've got a number of questions that I anticipate will take a little bit less than an hour. I would like to stress, sir, at the outset that it is not my intention in any way to confuse you, and so I would ask if any of my questions are unclear to you or you don't understand them, if you simply tell me that and I'll rephrase or reformulate the question so that you can understand it. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, yesterday, in response to some questions from Ms. Residovic, you told us about the presence of some MOS units, as you described them. And by "MOS," sir, were you referring to what was otherwise known as the Muslimanske Snage?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. In 1992, in the territory, in the field, they used the term MOS and the Muslim forces, but on the whole, this meant the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, if we're talking about the period -- let's talk about the last half of 1992, from, say, July to December 1992. Approximately, to the best of your knowledge, approximately how many people were in the MS or the MOS, in the area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. As I said, in the territory of Travnik municipality, well, I arrived there around the 21st of August. My unit arrived on the 25th of August. I had no information about the Muslim forces then, but later on I gained an impression, especially in the course of the defence of Karaula, and I think that that figure, for -- wasn't over a hundred. There weren't more than about a hundred Muslim troops in the area. Because in the Karaula area, there was a MOS detachment that was part of the defence and then it mysteriously disappeared. I think there were about 70 men in that unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, when you referred to them as a MOS detachment, were you aware or familiar about to whom these people reported or how they fit into any kind of a structure?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information about that. They weren't part of the structure that I was part of. That's certain. But they did exist, and they would appear in certain operations. They would say that they wanted to participate in combat action. And they engaged in combat operations on a sort of voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you say they would say that they wanted to participate in combat action, did you have any personal communication or interaction with any of the people from the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any personal communication with them, apart from the period in Karaula. I had contact with Commander Asim Koricic. He was part of the Muslim forces at the time. He was born in Bosnian Krajina, so it was on that basis we established contact. Some of his men were in a hamlet, in Karaula. So during that period, I had contact with him. I've told you about how I got to Bosnia, about my trip from Igman to Jajce, et cetera. So it was only on that occasion that I met them in the hamlet of Gradina, near Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, when you tell us that you had contact with Commander Asim Koricic, do you recall approximately when that was or on how many occasions you had contacts with Commander Koricic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was -- I'll try and be precise. Well, from the 6th of September up until the fall of Karaula, on the 15th of November, that's when we had contact. Because during certain periods of time, Karaula was a basis for combat action and for engaging in action in Jajce, and it was during that period that I had contact with Mr. Koricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, after the 15th of November, 1992, did you have any contacts with Asim Koricic?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was only after the 20th of January, because when the 3rd Corps command was formed, Mr. Koricic and some of those men who were members of the Muslim forces became part of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Zenica. So our ways separated. I remained in Travnik, he in Zenica. The first time I had contact with him was in January after my brigade had arrived at Visoko. Because part of the 7th was already in Visoko at the time. So that is where we met again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You said some of the members of the MOS, along with Mr. Koricic, became part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Do you know what happened to the members of the MOS who did not become part of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure. But on the basis of my experience, I could say that some of these men became part of the forces that didn't become part of any of the ABiH brigades, or rather, the 3rd Corps, and I've mentioned the villages in which this was the case; Mehurici, Orasac, et cetera. So I don't know how I would define these men. They were perhaps a little more extremist in a certain sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me again focus on -- your attention on the period in the autumn of 1992; that is, after your arrival in the Travnik area through November, December 1992. At that point in time, were you aware of where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the MOS had its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Let me repeat this: First of all, I wasn't from that area. I lived in a different republic. The command of the MOS was Mr. Koricic, who was in Karaula. But as for the other elements, I couldn't say anything about that. I knew that the Municipal Staff was in Travnik. There was Merdan in Zenica, but I didn't know anything about them. They weren't important. They had no effect on my combat operations or the situation in the zone of operations. This wasn't a respectable military force, so it wasn't necessary for me to have information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did -- during this time period, again, from your arrival in the area of Travnik until mid-November 1992, did the MOS wear any type of uniform or have any type of distinctive insignia that they wore on their clothing?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had uniforms. They had insignia. But it was a mixture. It wasn't as in the case of Territorial Defence units. Some had sabres as insignia, some had sort of Arabic inscriptions. I couldn't comment on that because I didn't understand it. But they didn't have the official insignia used by the Territorial Defence. They had crescents, they had stars, sabres as insignia, but the insignia used by the Territorial Defence, or rather, by the ABiH, was not the kind of insignia that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, the people who were part of this MOS, were those local Bosniaks or were they foreigners or was it a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were foreigners in the MOS. I apologise. They were Bosnians. As for the status of the foreigners at the time, I couldn't say anything about them. I don't know whether they were part of MOS, I don't know whether they were independent, and at the time, I wasn't interested in that. I didn't have opportunity of becoming interested in this because I was engaged in combat operations in a wide area. The ones I knew in MOS were Bosniaks; Koricic, Kokic, et cetera. A few people that I knew, but I didn't know any foreigners at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, other than Mr. Koricic and Mr. Kokic, do you recall the names of any of the soldiers or men who were part of the MOS?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because, as far as I know, at least, there were no people from the area of Bosnian Krajina among them, people that I might have known. Because I left my native town in 1971, I went to Belgrade, then I travelled all over Yugoslavia as part of my duty. So before the brigade was formed, I didn't even know the men that became members of my unit, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, was the term "MOS" used throughout 1993 or did that term fall out of use by the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when the Territorial Defence developed into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then terms like this ceased to be used by the Bosnian forces. On the other hand, the Chetnik propaganda machinery continued to call them the Muslim forces, et cetera, as you will see from the documents. And our ally, the HVO, in fact, introduced this term, the Muslim forces. So that it is possible that within army ranks and among Bosnians, this term had its reflections, but to a much lesser extent among the less educated people. But officially, it ceased to exist when the corps were formed. I must repeat: We didn't have educated officers, so that certain members may have used the term, but officially, it was not used, except for the 7th Brigade of the 3rd Corps, its name was the 7th Muslim Brigade. It was part of its name and it was the only one that had this prefix "Muslim."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know if that name came from the Muslim forces in the sense that Mr. Koricic went from being part of the MOS to being with the 7th and, as you told us, he took some of the soldiers with him? Was there a relation or a correlation between those facts?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really didn't understand that question. Could you be kind enough to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm not sure if I understood it either. Let me try again. You told us that Mr. Koricic had been the commander of the MOS and that he left the MOS and took some of the soldiers with him when the 7th Muslim Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I make a correction. He was not a commander of MOS, but one of the local commanders that I met on the ground. Who the main commander was, I don't know. So when the order was given to form the 3rd Corps and brigades, Koricic became part of the 7th Brigade with some of the men that went with him, and that became the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, the -- can you tell us what happened, to the best of your knowledge, to the municipal defence staffs once the 3rd Corps was formed. Did the municipal defence or regional defence staffs or local defence staffs continue to operate?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of the war was mainly based, after all, on the doctrines and combat rules of the former JNA, and with the formation of the corps and the brigades, the Territorial Defence staffs had a much less important role, linked to specific assignments within the territory, certain parts of the zones of operation. I cannot really talk about this, because my 17th Krajina Brigade was a manoeuvre brigade. I was not a local. Perhaps the commanders that had municipal staffs under them could tell you more about it. But anyway, in the chain of the command, the chain of command went from the corps to the brigades, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, once the operational groups were formed, did the orders go from the corps to the OGs to the brigades?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the Bosnian Krajina operations group, which was specific, the group was formed with the aim of integrating free manoeuvre forces to act towards Bosnian Krajina, because that is why it was called like that. And an organisational order said that the 17th, 305th, and the 7th should be a member of this operations group. But that never came to be. The orders did come through the command of the operations group, but these two brigades were still more or less directly linked to the corps commands. Maybe some parts of the 7th Brigade did function in that way, but the other operations groups were in a different position. But what would happen sometimes, due to specific situations, an order would be issued directly to the 17th Brigade, because they were re-subordinated to the Municipal Staff of Visoko. So that due to haste or specific situations, there were exceptions, but as a rule, the chain of command functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On several occasions, both yesterday as well as this afternoon, you have referred to the 17th Krajina Brigade as a manoeuvre brigade. I'm wondering if you can just tell us a little bit about the concept of a manoeuvre brigade and what exactly you mean by that term.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that there was a special concept of manoeuvre brigades, but the 17th Brigade was a brigade that did not consist of people from the local area but rather from people who came voluntarily from Western Europe to fight for their country and from people expelled from the territory of Bosnian Krajina. As for the method of use, it was used mostly for manoeuvre operations. If the situation in Visoko became difficult, then the corps commander would engage the 17th to assist there. Or if there were other such situations, the army was formed originally on a territorial principle. It's not a professional army. It was an army of workers and peasants, who didn't wish to leave their homes. The 17th had its own barracks, had conditions for training better than other units, and that is why we were used as a mobile manoeuvring unit most frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were there -- to your knowledge, were there other units or brigades or battalions within the 3rd Corps that you would characterise as being manoeuvre units?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not to the same extent, but the 7th Brigade could also be used as a manoeuvre brigade and the 305th from Jajce in the period 1992 to 1993. Later on, as things developed, as forces strengthened and all these measures were taken, I think that in 1993, 1994, parts of other units and entire units could be used outside their local municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you've mentioned the presence of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in Travnik. Can you tell us, during 1993, how frequently, if at all, that battalion operated in conjunction with or jointly with units of the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be as precise as I can in my answer. I think that throughout June 1993, we did act in conjunction with the 1st Battalion of the 7th. I have already said that part of that battalion was re-subordinated to the battalion at Bijelo Bucje so that in operations towards the HVO, Hajdarove Njive, Gradac, Dolac, and in a later stage, when the Chetniks tried to capture our lines at Bijelo Bucje and to gain control of Vilenica, a part of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade was used for a counter-attack and to gain control of Mradinska, Kamenjas features. I think that later on we linked up with Zenica, so that that battalion received orders more from the command in Zenica. So that -- I can't be quite sure, but I think that after September, or maybe December, there was no action in conjunction with the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have just a couple of follow-on questions, sir, based on your answer. You told us that part of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was re-subordinated to the battalion at Bijelo Bucje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, the battalion at Bijelo Bucje, can you be more precise about what battalion you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to my 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. So the 3rd Battalion of the 17th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell me also: You were shown yesterday Prosecution Exhibit P403, which referred to the 1st Sabotage Detachment. I'm not so much interested in that document, but if you recall the concept of sabotage detachments, if you could tell us a little bit about what a sabotage detachment is and what it does.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any sabotage detachment. Perhaps you're referring to an order in which the 17th is given the zone from Vlasic to Pakrac Stijene [phoen] with the counter-sabotage detachment. I don't think we were talking about a sabotage detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the usher if we could retrieve Prosecution Exhibit P403. And while that's being done, sir, we'll return to that subject in a moment. Let me ask you this: You told us yesterday about a number of units that were based in Travnik. The 17th Krajina Brigade, you told us, was headquartered in the former JNA barracks in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us earlier today that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was headquartered in the Medresa in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the command of the operation group Bosanska Krajina was also in the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, we're talking, sir, 1993. Can you tell us what other 3rd Corps units were in Travnik during 1993 and where those units had their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, in the town of Travnik itself, there was the command of the 312th Brigade. It is a domicile Travnik brigade which was headquartered in the building construction company in Travnik, included forces from the town of Travnik and from the local communities. In addition to that, in the territory of Travnik municipality, there was the 306th Brigade headquartered in the administration building of the mine at Han Bila. It consisted mainly of people from the Biljanska region and the Vlasic plateau. This is as far as Travnik municipality is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you now have Prosecution Exhibit P403 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 2(h). There's reference to the first PDO of Travnik. Do you see that reference, sir?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said that. Counter-sabotage detachment, not sabotage detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us -- thank you for that clarification. Can you please tell us what a counter-sabotage detachment, what its purpose was or its functions were?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say by way of introduction first that the 17th never took control of this zone, nor did this counter-sabotage detachment, was -- nor was it really subordinated to me, ever. I said that with the formation of the corps command, the main forces of the corps are brigades, and they account for the bulk of the manpower of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they were formed on the territorial principle, as I have already described for the 17th, the 7th, and the Jajce Brigade, which was left without its territory, but the manpower came from Jajce. As far as my memory serves me, according to the doctrine of the former JNA, a counter-sabotage detachment, as elements of the structure of the Territorial Defence, were meant to engage in counter-sabotage battle, to prevent infiltration of enemy, terrorist forces, to control the territory, and they are given auxiliary tasks in battle; control of the areas in between zones, to protect command posts, important economic facilities, which could be the target of sabotage activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I may, let me add: The intention of the corps commander probably was to relieve the brigade of these subsidiary activities so that we could focus on our primary mission against the Chetniks, thereby the operative units would have greater freedom of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to a few questions about the people that we've referred to - and actually, the usher can retrieve that document - the people that we've referred to a few times during your testimony as the Mujahedin. Now, you told us, sir, yesterday about a situation where one of your soldiers had been kidnapped by these foreigners. I believe you told us that he maybe had had a little too much to drink and they took him to their camp. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's a part of your testimony I'd like to ask you about, and this is from yesterday's transcript, at page 51, lines 17 through 19. And you said, or the English translation of your testimony said, and I'm quoting: "I sent a direct message via certain Islamic circles in Travnik, and the message was that my weapons are turned towards their camp and that I would attack them if they didn't send my soldier free."

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: When you say, "I sent a direct message via certain Islamic circles in Travnik," can you elaborate on that or tell us a little bit about what you meant when you said "certain Islamic circles in Travnik"?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent my commander of an artillery division to contact the mufti of Travnik and to talk to him. As he was rather resolute and rather firm and convincing, to ask the mufti kindly to let those gentlemen, or rather, brothers, as they called them, know of this message, and obviously the message reached them. Because my estimate was that, as a religious officer, he probably had some contact with them. Because through official military channels, it was not possible to deblock him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the name of the mufti of Travnik that you sent your artillery division commander to speak to?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the battalion, not division. Redzic Asmir. He was directly subordinated to me. Of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I mean the person Mr. Redzic Asmir, you sent him to speak to the mufti of Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's still the mufti. Nusret Efendija Avdibegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So I take it, then, from the fact that you passed on this message that your weapons were turned on their camp, that had an impact upon them releasing your soldier?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at first. A couple of hours later, and I said yesterday the delegation arrived at my barracks, asked to be received by me. We spent more than two hours in difficult discussions, and this resulted in them apologising and releasing this soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you just mentioned that a delegation arrived at your barracks. Do you recall any of the people who were part of this delegation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I will remember most of them, at least those whose names I know. There was the mentioned mufti, then the president of the municipality, Curic, because in the meantime, he learnt of the tense situation and the possibility of the worst happening. Then, on behalf of the Mujahedin, Abu Haris, an Arab who spoke Bosnian well, and an emir of theirs, I don't remember his name, but in translation, emir means commander, and Mr. Meqtauf in the role of interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to -- let me ask you first about Abu Haris, an Arab who, as you put it, spoke Bosnian well. Did you know Abu Haris prior to the time he came to meet you to discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because we had occasion to meet earlier on, so I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, do you recall approximately how many times you either encountered Abu Haris or spoke to Abu Haris?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say during 1993. I met Abu Haris for the first time, and this was my first direct contact with an Arab, sometime around the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 10th of September. Because, by decision of Commander El Mujahed [realtime transcript read in error "Elmu"], they were ordered to participate with the 17th Brigade, so that Abu Haris was the contact, the interpreter between me and my officers and parts of the El Mujahed unit. And then in the following ten days, there were several contacts, maybe every two or three days we had contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what precisely, if you know, was Abu Haris's role within the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to tell you what the exact roles were, not just as far as Abu Haris is concerned but the others too, because they were not structured in any logical way, in our view. So that he was introduced to me as an interpreter in the detachment. Now, whether he had any important role in that detachment, believe me, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also just told us by decision of Commander -- and then the transcript lost the name. It says "Commander Elmu." They were ordered to the participate in the 17th Brigade. Do you recall the name of the commander who made this decision?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superior was the commander of the operations group, Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I want to be absolutely clear here, sir, without any confusion. Did Commander Alagic issue the order that they were to, as you put it, participate with the 17th Brigade or is there some confusion here?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no confusion. At the beginning of September, I'm not sure of the date, but Mr. Alagic issued the order that they should participate with the 17th in this combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which year was this, sir? September of which year?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 1993. Because in 1992 there was no operations group, or in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also mentioned as part of this delegation, and let's return now to the delegation that came to see you concerning your soldier who had been kidnapped - you mentioned Mr. Meqtauf as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Meqtauf prior to that day or had you had any encounters with him prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally. I just knew that he had a winery [as interpreted] called Palma. It was in the centre of town, and I knew the owner was Meqtauf. I don't know anything about him, anything special about him. At this meeting, he appeared as a member of the delegation and acted as interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe there might be an error in the English transcript. It says that Mr. Meqtauf had a winery called Palma. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A video club. Meqtauf is an Arab. He doesn't drink wine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's why I needed to clarify that, sir. Now, Mr. Meqtauf, after this time when he came as part of this delegation as an interpreter, did you see him or encounter him at any point after this point in time during the war? I'm not talking about if you ever saw him in his video shop, but during the war did you have any subsequent encounters or meetings where Mr. Meqtauf was present?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even in the video club. Because I didn't have enough time to spend time in town. On the whole, I was with my unit in the field, in the zone of operations. I never had the opportunity of meeting Meqtauf again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also mentioned yesterday - and again, this is page 50, lines 16 through 18 - that in dealing with the El Mujahed detachment or unit, that you had to use negotiation teams, as you put it yesterday. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, I said after its formation, in order to use the El Mujahed detachment, or part of it, some delegations had to ensure that they would accept this. Maybe that's what you are referring to. So it wasn't as if they were units of any other kind. It's not as if the commander could issue an order and be sure that commanders of subordinate units would take all the measures necessary to carry out the task as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just read out part of the English version of the transcript and see if this accurately captured your testimony yesterday. This is page 50, beginning at the end of line 16, and you're referring to or your discussing the El Mujahed detachment. And it says the following: "But when they were formed, when this unit was formed, you always had to use negotiation teams to see if they would participate in actions or not, to see whether they would receive any markings."

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, signals, you know, some sort of a sign. But on the whole, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience. I'm providing you with this answer on the basis of my experience and on the basis of my information. I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: Based on your experience and the basis of your information, how many of the people within the El Mujahed detachment spoke the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only Abu Haris did, as far as I know. He was in that detachment. There were some Bosniaks in that detachment who spoke the Bosnian language, and some of them probably spoke Arabic too. I don't know all the details. But I only know that Abu Haris could speak the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that because not everyone in that unit spoke Bosnian, that there were certain language barriers in communicating with people in that detachment?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a logical conclusion, but I couldn't say. I wasn't in the detachment. I don't know about these linguistic barriers. But as far as these foreigners are concerned, all I know is that Abu Haris could speak the Bosnian language. Perhaps there were Bosniaks who had studied in Arabic countries, Bosniaks who were imams, et cetera. So perhaps this enabled them to communicate. But I don't know anything about this, so I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any point in the spring or summer of 1993, did you become aware that the Mujahedin in the camp near Mehurici were holding civilians?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you tell me about the period again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the spring or summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I neglected, sir, to ask you earlier a couple of questions concerning the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. You told us that during certain parts of 1993, including June of 1993 and onwards, that battalion operated frequently with the 17th Krajina Brigade. And my question, sir, is: Do you recall the name of the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade during the time period that that battalion or parts thereof operated jointly with your brigade?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Safet Junuzovic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, do you recall the name of any of the commander of the companies that formed the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade during the period that they operated with units of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, and I may be mistaken, I can remember Suad Jusufovic. He was from Kozarac, which is the place of my birth. That's why I remember his name. I can't remember the names of the others. These were new men. So I can't even remember the names of my company commanders from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during 1993, do you recall the approximate number of foreign fighters that could be characterised as Mujahedin who were present in the area around Travnik and Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anyone had that kind of information at the time. We made certain assessments. At one point in time, it was decided that they should be monitored. But I don't think there could have been more than about a hundred of them in Travnik municipality. And together with the men from the territory of Bosnia, maybe 200 of them. But I can't be sure. I couldn't say that's the absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay, sir. You just told us that at one point in time, it was decided that they should be monitored. Do you know if they were in fact monitored?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 7th Corps was disbanded in February 1996. I became deputy commander of the 5th Corps. So I know that the security service monitored them. I don't know whether they pulled them or not. My organs, and at my level of command, this was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, sir, to avoid confusion, when you said earlier "it was decided that they should be monitored," when was that decision taken? What time period, roughly?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was it in 1993 or was it much later?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Look, we were fighting for our survival. We were training. We were fighting against two aggressors, et cetera. This was a lot later. After all the problems that they caused in the territory, the security department, or state security, according to the information I have, they were engaged in an operation and they monitored them. But I can't be precise. I wasn't part of the plan. I didn't participate in it. I wasn't involved in an analysis of this matter. So what I'm saying is on the basis of what the media reported later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, as you put it, you were fighting for your survival at this point in time in 1993. Did the Mujahedin make a contribution in that fight for survival?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that I look back at the time, well, it's possible to make assessments then. But at the time, they were allies in a certain sense. They contributed to our survival. And given the way in which the international community and the neighbours of ours were behaving, given the way the Republic of Croatia was behaving, and in 1992, they provided us with a lot of assistance, well, a lot of our people, you know, in Travnik, Zenica, these are poor areas, so a lot of our people in those areas thought that these foreigners had come to help them. They -- this turned out to be different later on, but I think that on the whole, they did contribute to our fight for survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of how these foreigners, these Mujahedin, came into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know. They could have only come in via Croatia, through Herceg-Bosna, the so-called Herceg-Bosna, either as part of certain missions, humanitarian missions, perhaps, or because they were engaged in certain services, certain departments. I don't know. But they did arrive in the territory of Central Bosnia, and they didn't arrive by air; they arrived by land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1992, isn't it true that the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats were fighting together against the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, in Central Bosnia and elsewhere in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, up to a certain point in time, yes. But at the end of 1992, and this is something I could see in the documents shown to me yesterday, by autumn 1992, the HVO was treating us as an enemy army. But let me repeat this. I have to be quite frank. I formed a volunteer unit in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia provided me with a lot of assistance. I received a salary from the Republic of Croatia, and this continued up until November 1992. In September 1993, my family had to leave Varazdin. They had to leave the Republic of Croatia. Something changed, and this was wasn't up to the soldiers. This is something that happened at a political level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, again, sir, I'd like to focus on the middle part of 1992, right after the war in Bosnia broke out. At that point in time, in the summer and into the early part of autumn, August, September, of 1992, the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats were fighting together against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, yes. But in certain municipalities, even in June 1992, there was tension, especially in the municipalities in the Lasva Valley, in Busovaca, in Novi Travnik, and in Vitez. But on the whole, generally speaking, this is true, from the Neretva valley, into Jajce, into Posavina, in these areas, the Bosnians and -- or rather the Bosniaks and the Croats fought against the Chetniks. Up until October 1992. In October, the situation changed. Prozor was attacked. Then after the fall of Jajce and Bosanski Brod -- well, you can see from the documents shown yesterday that we were then treated as an enemy army. We were under a blockade. There was a lot of looting, et cetera. And this is something that can be seen in the documents shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I just have one more question before we take our first technical break. I suggest to you, sir, that the primary reason the Mujahedin came to Bosnia was to fight against the Serbs. Do you care to comment on that statement?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have a lot of respect for your opinion. However, on the basis of my experience, I would say that they came to help their Muslim brothers, and I believe that about -- well, almost all of them had an idea who the Chetniks were. That's what happened in the initial stage. Later on, they assumed a missionary role. They were spreading their religion, their customs. They tried to prevent people from drinking alcohol. I don't want to go into all of that, because we could talk about this for a long time. Their main role was to help the Muslim in Bosnia and Herzegovina in their help for survival and the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that that was their purpose in 1992. But later on, this role changed. They assumed a different kind of role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President. I would expect that I have about 15 to 20 more minutes, depending on, of course, of the answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our break now and we will resume at about five to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the break I was reviewing my notes and I neglected to ask you a couple of questions concerning the time where one of your soldiers was kidnapped by the Mujahedin. So I'd like to return very briefly to that subject, if I might. Can you please tell us the degree to which Mr. Salko Beba was involved in the negotiations or discussions with the Mujahedin for the release of the soldier that they had kidnapped from your brigade.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. I can't tell you exactly, because Salko Belga [as interpreted] was an organ within the organisations group. I informed the OG, but it didn't work, so then I decided that since a member of my unit was at risk, I acted as I did. I thought I had the right to do so. Salko Beba was in the security department of the OG, but I was in the field, and Beba wasn't my responsibility, so I can't really answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, then, Witness, you're not aware of any efforts of Mr. Salko Beba to secure the release of the soldier from your brigade who had been kidnapped by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that he made efforts, but as to what he did and to what degree, all I know is that it didn't bear any fruit. It was his responsibility to deal with such problems, but he was not under my command and he didn't report to me. These efforts didn't bear any fruit, so I proceeded in the way that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to turn to a completely different topic now. You told us yesterday, page 21, lines 8 through 11, about visiting your family in Croatia. And I have a few questions about this. The transcript reads: "Often I would go to Croatia to visit my family, who had remained in --" I believe it was Rastinja [phoen].

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Varazdin. Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Varazdin. So your family remained in Varazdin. Can you tell us the time period when you said yesterday, "Often I would go to visit my family in Croatia," what time period were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell you the months. I visited my family in August on one occasion, once in October, and once at the beginning of December, and the last time was between February and March. So I visited them on four or five occasions. But since we were living in wartime conditions, I think that I visited them quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say August, October, and December, I take it that was 1992?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, and end of February and beginning of March in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you travelled to Croatia on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in August I went there in a jeep. In October, in a passenger vehicle, a private vehicle. I apologise. I went there by bus, by train. I went there by train and I came back by bus. In December I went there by bus, and in March I returned by a passenger car which was taken away from me at a checkpoint by the HVO and then continued to Travnik by bus from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You also made reference on page 21 yesterday, line 9, the testimony was: "My combatants would return from medical treatment from London, from Croatia." I'm wondering again if you could tell us what the time period was where soldiers from your brigade went abroad for medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was up until October. The hospital in Split, in Firule, I think there was a lieutenant colonel from the JNA who was born in Bosanska Krajina. And he made sure that our wounded men would be received there and that they would be provided with medical treatment in Split. There were other channels that were used, through the Merhamet Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. charity organisation in Zagreb, for example. At the beginning of October, I don't know exactly how, but there was a man of ours in Ljubljana. We managed to return or rather send about 30 wounded men to London for medical treatment. There wasn't -- there weren't many medical supplies in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The hospitals were poorly equipped and poorly staffed. And some men would return from abroad and join the units again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, when you say October, can you tell us what year?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now a couple of questions about something that again you told us yesterday, page 28, lines 2 through 4. You made reference to being present at a meeting in Travnik in mid-October 1992, when the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, was in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That meeting started in Plava Voda, in Travnik, and because of the shelling, they probably intercepted some sort of telephone conversation. But we soon moved to Han Bila, and that's where most of the meeting was held. It was mostly held in Han Bila, and I attended the meeting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, due to the timing of that meeting, that was prior to the establishment of the 3rd Corps and its units?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date, but it was before the fall of Jajce, in mid-October, Jajce fell on the 30th of October, and one of the issues discussed was the defence of Jajce. I remember that individual commanders made statements. It was in mid-October. I don't know whether it was the 14th, 15th, or 16th, but it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, sir, the individual commanders made statements, do you know what units those commanders represented at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll mention the ones I remember, the ones I know. Commanders of municipal defence staffs from Travnik, Jajce, Bugojno, assisted. The commanders of the Krajina unit, of the 1st Krajina Battalion, of the 7th Krajina Battalion, who were present. We gave a brief briefing to President Izetbegovic on the situation in the province. We asked for assistance when dealing with certain problems, et cetera. And we were given certain instructions too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if anyone from the MOS or Muslim forces was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already said there were commanders of municipal staffs, commanders of units. I know who was there from the Krajina unit, but as for the Muslim forces, as far as I know, no one was present; none of them were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to draw your attention to your testimony yesterday concerning measures that were taken by your brigade when you became aware of crimes committed by soldiers of the 17th Krajina Brigade. Yesterday you told us about remanding soldiers for disciplinary violations. Do you remember testifying about this issue?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the soldiers who were charged with disciplinary violations during the time period you were the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of names. Perhaps I can remember their nicknames rather than their names. I can't remember that many names, but there was Koljic, Rokic [phoen], Nakic, then -- just a minute. Fazlic, Savic, Sivac, Alic. These are just some of names I can remember. These were people from my area, so that I can remember them more easily. Because all the men in my brigade were new. There were 2.000 men and a brigade commander can't know all of their names. But these are some of the names that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the specific disciplinary offences or crimes that these -- any of these individuals were investigated for or charged with?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, there were disciplinary offences, misdemeanours, for which investigations were conducted and measures were taken. There were offences, there were misdemeanours, and there were crimes which were sanctioned in accordance with the Penal Code. But as far as disciplinary mistakes are concerned, well, this happened at the beginning, on the whole, because the members of my brigade weren't well educated. Some people would -- some men would spend money intended for certain purposes on alcohol. There was a lack of discipline in the sense of failure to carry out orders, in the sense of not going to training, in the sense of opposing one's superiors. Food was stolen. The situation was difficult at that time. People had been expelled to a small area. It was difficult to feed one's family. So we made efforts to create a normal system of discipline which would enable the unit to function. As for more serious disciplinary offences, all that included acts that people committed when under the influence of alcohol. They would open fire in the town. They would commit offences in the dormitories, in the barracks. When the conflict broke out, well, there was an example yesterday, other people's property was stolen. There was theft. Buildings were set on fire. So you had whole range of offences. You had lighter offences and you had more serious offences, and we took measures on the basis of the acts committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about the incidents involving theft, which you just mentioned. Do you recall the specific locations where any thefts occurred that you had soldiers of your brigade investigated?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Yesterday there was a concrete example of Muharem Koljic. He took a sack of flour from an abandoned Croat house and there was criminal charges against him. Then there was Nukic, who ended up in prison for 90 days because of a sack of flour. 60 days of prison, because he stole a sack of flour for his own family. Those are two examples that come to mind. These thefts mostly occurred from abandoned houses, at night, in the villages, or from stores that were abandoned, and supplies were simply stolen. And when we discovered such offences, we took steps against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, sir: You also mentioned buildings were set on fire. Again, do you recall the specific locations where buildings were set on fire and soldiers of the 17th Krajina Brigade were subsequently investigated for such fires?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that any member of the 17th was charged with burning, with torching. But there were cases that members of my unit would catch civilians torching, and then my security service would file charges with the authorities. I remember a Bosniak from Toca [phoen] was sentenced to a couple of years in prison for torching abandoned Croat houses. So, to be quite frank, I can't recollect any example from my own brigade. But from the documents we saw yesterday, there were more than a hundred disciplinary measures enforced in the first six months. I'm just repeating that I can't remember. I do know of this case that my military police submitted charges against this person. I don't think he was a member of the unit, but he was a local man, in fact, a rather well-off man, who was charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, finally, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the checkpoint incident that you told us about yesterday that occurred, as you put it, on the greatest Muslim holiday. You spoke about this yesterday. It's recorded at page 35, lines 6 through 14 of the trial testimony. At the time of this incident, sir, can you tell us what type of clothing you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, I was wearing the American alpha summer uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the other individuals who were with you in the vehicle, what type of clothing were they wearing, or were you by yourself on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a van and a vehicle. There was a band in the van, and in the vehicle, there was Alagic, myself, the driver, and maybe a military policeman. And we were all wearing camouflage uniforms with regular army insignia. There were no ranks then. But I didn't mention it yesterday. To make things even more absurd, that very day, in Travnik, I think it was in the motel, with HVO commanders who were our guests at the Bajram celebrations, and after we had taken our separate ways, said goodbye, only a few minutes later we suffered such humiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, the people who were manning the checkpoint were HVO soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We know them. It was the so-called Tuka's Group. Tuka was a member of the special police of the HVO, and he often was involved in such incidents. And as far as I know, I think he was killed in some sort of settling of accounts among two HVO members during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these members of this so-called Tuka's group, at the time you encountered them at this checkpoint, were they also wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. There wasn't a standing, a permanent checkpoint. It was a checkpoint formed especially for us. It was a side-road. It wasn't on the main road. There was a checkpoint at the crossroads. But this was a side-road going from Travnik, via Skokovi, Ilovaca, Bunarevo, through the Slimena village. So it was formed probably on the basis of some information received. So it was a planned ambush, in fact. They were pointing their weapons at us and we were surrounded on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this incident that you're telling us about took place, if I remember correctly, on or about the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, in the early evening. Because during the day, we were attending the celebrations at the hotel, and in the evening, we had planned some cultural event and we were on our way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time, and I mean on the 1st of June, 1993, the ABiH and the HVO were in effect fighting each other in the Lasva and Bila River Valleys; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The conflict, the Ahmici occurred on the 16th of April, and after that, a cease-fire was ordered by the superior command. And we abided by this truce. On the 19th of April, there was a trial attack, but it was stopped, and then later on there were constant negotiations to prevent a conflict. A joint command was formed at the post office in Travnik. There were plans made, and through this operational plan, we sought to avoid a conflict, but it wasn't implemented, and a conflict broke out. But at that time, there were no planned combat operations. Because, I repeat: We were with the Leotar, Rasa Filipovic at this Bajram reception together on that same day, so we were shocked by this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have a few questions for you. I will have a series of questions for you. Unless the Defence has some additional questions on the basis of the cross-examination of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do have several questions for the general.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you were explaining the way army units were used, and you showed us how your brigade, which consisted of persons who were refugees or volunteers from abroad, were put up in barracks and took part in certain combat operations. In answer to a question by my learned friend, you said that -- you told us, to the best of your recollection, when you acted together with a part of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade. My question is: Can you remember whether your unit or parts of your unit, including parts of the 7th Brigade, were also involved in operations outside the area of the 3rd Corps, when dramatic events occurred around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time of the Chetnik offensive along the axis Rogoj-Trnovo-Igman sometime in August 1993, because of the critical situation when Igman was about to fall, which would mean a twofold, a double blockade of Sarajevo, on the basis of the command of the 3rd Corps, the 1st Battalion, I think, a battalion of the 7th Muslim, was used. This gentleman Jusovic went, I know. It was not just my unit, but a temporary composition was formed of the operations group, headed by Salkic, from Travnik. So parts from the 312th Brigade, my 4th Battalion, and some people from Jajce. So this Bosanska Krajina detachment did participate in saving Igman and halting the Chetniks, together with the forces of the 7th Muslim. So these were forces from the operations group, and this was in the month of August. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend drew your attention to a part of your response yesterday, referring to efforts being made to give orders to El Mujahed and that at the time, you actually had to negotiate with them, that they had to be appealed to, and that they didn't really accept command in the way other units do. In that part of the transcript, referred to by my learned friend, you said that they were clearly not under control and command. So, in view of that question, I would like to ask you: Those negotiations and discussions with El Mujahed and their representatives, were they the reason -- were these due to the fact that they couldn't speak the language properly or was it because, what you said earlier on, they refused the command and control of the army command.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just repeat the last part of your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend discussed with you the question that among the foreigners there were many who couldn't speak our language, and he asked you whether this caused some misunderstanding in communication. I am asking you whether what you were saying yesterday, that is, the need to debate with them every single order, to negotiate with them, to appeal to them, was that due to the fact that they didn't understand the language or was it due to the fact that even in those days, they would not accept the command and control of the army command?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with language problems. It was more a general attitude that they had towards the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we could frequently hear them saying that the army was lay [as interpreted], that it was full of communists, that we were not real Muslims and so on. Generally you could give them an order, but if they did not agree to carry it out, nothing came of it. So they carried out only those orders which, on the basis of some signs of theirs or prayers or whatever, they agreed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that matter has now been fully clarified. As for the part of the discussion you had with my learned friend about the reason that prompted them to come in 1992 and your response that they probably came to assist their Muslim brothers, tell me, please: This frustration of the ordinary Bosniak who felt that he was betrayed first by his neighbours and then by Europe and the rest of the world, was this feeling of frustration a fertile soil for these Mujahedin to have significant influence among the ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. And let me repeat that in this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the areas that they settled in in 1993, and generally speaking, under conditions of a struggle for survival, many of us are ready to accept the devil himself if he will help you. So it's understandable that they were treated and accepted as allies, as people who would help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with that question, are you aware, General -- let me rephrase that. After the formation of the 17th Krajina Brigade, did that brigade ever act together with the Mujahedin in any kind of combat operation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, at the beginning of September 1993, we did have a joint operation towards Vitez, the area of Kruscica, with a part of that El Mujahed detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But my question is: Before the formation of the El Mujahed, did you ever have any connection with those Mujahedin that were situated in the area?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the order that you received from General Alagic, and now you added to it by saying that those foreigners were involved in a combat operation with you in September. Tell me: How did they behave during that battle? Did they accept command or did they act according to their own free will?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can say with full responsibility that my experience on the basis of that operation is extremely negative, because regardless of the plan of the operation, the issued order, and everything else, because we had done our best to prepare it properly, during the operation itself, they acted independently, and this caused considerable losses in my own unit. That day, I think I had 78 wounded and 16 dead, which had never happened to me as a brigade commander up until then, nor after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
