utterances.text: Thank you. I have just a few more questions linked to measures taken by you, as discussed by my learned friend. You told us what your attitude was towards the discipline of soldiers and how measures were taken against anyone committing any kind of disciplinary offence or crime, and you said you did the same in relation to a relative of yours, if I understood you correctly. Tell me: What was the position of your superior command and Commander Alagic towards the perpetrators of criminal acts and any disciplinary offenders?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did, I did on the basis of orders, instructions, regulations, and the law. Therefore, Mr. Alagic was very explicit and strict in that respect. He demanded from his subordinates that every measure should be taken. And some measures were taken on the basis of things he himself saw. I personally remember an event, I think near Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Guca Gora, when he saw a member of the 306th Brigade driving away property from a Croatian house, and he put him in gaol. Therefore, there's no need to comment on his attitude towards these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you knew Commander Alagic very well, as you cooperated with him directly, could you tell me: In accordance with the orders you received, in accordance with the reports that you needed to submit, and the control over the execution of orders, what was the position of the commander of the 3rd Corps with respect to the investigation of crimes and the perpetrators of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know what his attitude was, because Commander Alagic was named commander of the operations group at the end of February, so that we were directly on the line. And through his instructions, through the assignments we received at briefings, through written documents and a very resolute attitude about training and taking of measures against all negative tendencies, it is not up to me to judge my superiors, but my conviction is that he was very resolute in ordering and taking measures against perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked whether you can remember the names of persons who were disciplined and charged. I am asking you: In your experience, did you have an occasion when a soldier or an officer who committed an offence or a crime, do you know of any case when he was pardoned and allowed to go unpunished?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no case when no measures were taken. If there was knowledge about an act, then disciplinary measures and charges were issued. But about -- I did have the position to pardon after two thirds of the sentence had been served. So if soldiers showed remorse, then they could be pardoned, but they were always sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think, General, that brings to an end my questions, and thank you for answering them for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cuskic, in answer to a question from my learned friend, you said the incident at the checkpoint occurred on the 1st of June, wasn't it, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out between the HVO and the ABiH, you were in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, can you remember where you were?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was in Travnik on that day too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A second point I would like us to clear up a little is, when you said that the 7th Muslim Brigade was the only one that had this prefix, and I think you were referring only to brigades within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was one with that prefix in the 4th Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I was to tell you that there were some in the 1st Corps, in the 6th Corps, in the 4th Corps, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you. That is correct. I think that in every corps there was a brigade carrying that prefix.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Just one further point. Answering questions about the MOS, or the Muslim forces. Yesterday, during your testimony, on page 48, line 19 to 49, you said that at the time the corps and brigades were formed, the Territorial Defence and a part of the MOS became part of operational units or units of the Territorial Defence that remained under the command of the municipal staffs. My question is: When a corps or a brigade was being formed, members of the MOS join not only the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade, but they also joined other units of the ABiH, organised in Travnik, the 306th Brigade, the 312th, the 314th?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. That is the gist of the answer that I gave that you quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As I was saying a moment ago, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be kind enough to return to the beginning of what you said yesterday regarding the Mujahedin and Karaula. This is on page 48, line 2. You said that the Mujahedin participated in the defence of Karaula. Are you confirming that? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A group of Mujahedin, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you yourself, were you at Karaula at the same time as they were there?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not throughout. At the time, they were located in a hamlet called Gradula [phoen], this group of Mujahedin. It wasn't a big group. And I would pass through Karaula and I would spend some time there, but it was the last group of villages between the municipality of Travnik and Jajce. This was intended to be of assistance to Jajce. So that when going to Jajce, I would pass through there, and in the period from the 6th of September until around the 15th of November, 1992, I would be there on and off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Mujahedin, therefore, were present in this location between the month of September and November 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Independently of them, were there other forces and other units present with them alongside with them, around them, or were they alone facing the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Karaula, as a group of villages, there was the Karaula detachment under the command of the Municipal Staff of Travnik, and the numerical strength was about 1.100 men. So a part of my unit, certain logistic elements for communications were there and that would roughly be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are confirming that there were soldiers belonging to your unit who were present there. These Mujahedin, they came of their own [as interpreted], who asked them to come? Because in theory, you controlled the area. What were they doing there? Did you need them?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, how they came, I can't tell you, because they got there before me. I controlled that territory from the 8th to the 15th of November, when I was in charge of the defence of Karaula. And those 1.100 men who were on a front of 36 kilometres had at the beginning no more than a hundred rifles. And anyone coming with a weapon is welcome if he can defend his home and his village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. We are learning that there was a 36-kilometre-long front line and there were the Mujahedin on one side and the Serbs on the other. Did you have any contact with the Mujahedin on the ground? How did you control the operations on the ground? Because combatants wearing uniforms, how can you distinguish -- how could you distinguish between -- how could you share out the territory?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you didn't understand me too well. I repeat: I reached Karaula on the 5th or 6th of September. I was engaged to assist the Jajce municipality. The group of Mujahedin were located in a hamlet called Gradina. My combat experiences with them are the following: If I am attacking -- if we agree that they should participate, I allocate them a hill so they can be separate, isolated, for several reasons, because of language, for recognition, because of communications. We had no radio stations, no telephone, no communication. And my experience is limited to the defence of Karaula. This period from the 10th to the 15th of November, we really did take part together in the defence of Karaula and we failed. They were not always with my units every day in the period from September to mid-November, maybe in two battles we acted together. Nor did I have any communication with them in the sense of issuing orders to them. I was doing my part of the work towards Jajce and the Chetniks. I don't know if I've managed to clarify this. I hope I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to another operation in response to a question put to you by the Defence. You said that in September, in the Vitez area, there was a joint operation with a Mujahedin unit. Are you quite sure that this took place in September?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure. It was on the 18th of September, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of September, on the 18th of September, and a little earlier, you mentioned Mount Igman. Is that in the same area?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Igman is a mountain near Sarajevo. It's over a hundred kilometres from Vitez. And this took place when we sent a detachment from Bosnian Krajina in August. This was on the 18th of September, this event we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You say that you sent a detachment in August to Mount Igman. Who was on Mount Igman then?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Bosanska Krajina and a joint detachment sent this detachment. They were from the 312th from the 17th, I think there were some men from Jajce, and the defence of Igman was under the 1st Sarajevo Corps. They were responsible for the defence. And I think it was Mr. Karavelic who was the commander at the time. I don't know the exact details. I wasn't there myself. Mr. Salkic from Travnik was the detachment commander, and he was subordinated to the 1st Corps. But I know that he was successful in carrying out his operation, and the 1st Corps commander praised him for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on Mount Igman, as far as you know, did the 7th Brigade also participate in operations there or not?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in response to a question from Defence counsel, I already said that the 3rd Corps sent a battalion from the 7th Muslim Brigade, and a joint detachment from Bosanska Krajina. They were to assist the 1st Corps in defending Igman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, in the 7th Brigade Battalion, were there any elements from the El Mujahed unit or were there any Mujahedin, on the basis of what you know?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because their units were led by Jusovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now ask the registrar to produce the B/C/S version of document 616. I'm going to show you a document which is in your language. The copy is not very good, but could you please have a look at the document. Could you please read it. Could you tell us who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was drafted by Ahmet Adilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which unit did Ahmet Adilovic belong to?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which unit he belonged to. I know that he was an imam in Travnik and he was the director of the Medresa. As to the unit he was a member of, I couldn't say. He wasn't a very prominent person, or perhaps he was, but he wasn't in contact with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who -- well, so you know this person. You know Mr. Adilovic. Who is this document addressed to?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to the 3rd Corps command, to the operations group, to the operations department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what is the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a request for a helicopter flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's a request for a helicopter. On whose behalf was this request made?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was drafted by the gentleman in question, but you can't see whether these individuals -- well, it says we know 11 individuals. They are Arabs and Turks who should go to Igman. I don't think that this document is formulated in military terms. You can't see which structure is involved and the vocabulary -- well, it says transport them by helicopter and it should be used for one or two flights. But the vocabulary used doesn't seem to be military. The document is inconsistent, and it's not a military-type document. So the document really doesn't merit military comments of any kind. Because the 3rd Corps command issued a precise order in which they stated how a helicopter would be requested. You would have to mention the coordinates, you would have to mention the place where the helicopter was supposed to land, you would have to mention the time, the landing point, et cetera. I've used helicopters to transport the wounded from Kruscica to Zenica, so this is how I know about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that you don't understand why 11 Arabs or Turks should go to Igman by helicopter following a request within the 3rd Corps. You can't explain this?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got an explanation to provide because army helicopters were used for the purposes of other transports in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this group certainly didn't participate in stopping the Chetnik attack on Igman. Because our units were transferred via Fojnica, Tarcin, they participated in combat -- well, I think this was before this date. I think the attack had been stopped before this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that Ahmet Adilovic was someone you knew, but he was an imam and not a member of the military. On the 27th of August, 1993, he didn't have a military status?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying. I know that he was an imam and that he was the director of the Medresa in Travnik. But I couldn't say that he was a member of the army or not. I know that he was an imam in Travnik. He was the director of the Medresa, and that is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know understand why an imam would make a request, would request that the military authorities provide a helicopter; you can't provide us with an explanation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says that the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, well, this still wouldn't have been his responsibility, though. Only a corps commander can sign such documents. The battalion command isn't responsible for communicating with the corps command, let alone an officer for moral guidance. As a soldier, I don't understand this. And in military terms, this is a document which is quite illiterate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take the document from you. You can take the floor in a minute. I'll go on to another subject now. If I have understood you correctly, you were the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade; is that correct? From January to December 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add something. From the time it was formed on the 25th of November, 1992, up until the 7th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you weren't on the battlefield, as commander, where was your office located? Where was your office?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was in the centre of the brigade command, on the top floor, behind the stage in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this brigade command, which town was it located in?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Travnik. The building of the brigade command. The command of the brigade was engaged as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wasn't it in the former JNA barracks, or what we call the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That's what I'm saying. It was in the barracks. There was the central stage and it was to the rear, on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June 1993, as far as you know, were there any prisoners who were detained in the former JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These prisoners, who was responsible for these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 3rd Corps command regulated the situation, and before the commission for POWs was formed, naturally, I was the person who was most responsible for them, but I assigned this responsibility to Colonel Dedic Salko. He was my assistant for morale. He would monitor the situation and report to me on the situation. As far as controlling the situation, monitoring them, naturally it was the military security department and the military police who were responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an officer who was responsible for the situation, did you ever visit the prisoners of war? Did you visit the individuals who were detained?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't pay them a visit to visit them for this sole purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't see them?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did see them, but I didn't plan visits to them, because there were other reasons for which I would go to that area, so perhaps I passed through and saw them when passing through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you saw them, none of them complained about being maltreated, about being beaten, none of them complained about the living conditions? This never took place?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So everything was fine? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, everything was fine. And according to reports from the International Red Cross when visiting -- when the 3rd Corps command visited them, when Mr. Pavo Nikolic visited them, everyone established that the situation was fine. And as I said, the conditions that my soldiers had when detained were the conditions that POWs lived in too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know why these people were detained? What were they charged with?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The detainees, why were they detained? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I explained that, on the first, second, and third day of the conflict with the HVO, we had 40 POWs. After investigations had been conducted by the security body, and after a report, according to which about ten of them had been imprisoned in the houses in Slimena, these houses were the first to be attacked, I then ordered that these people should be released. As for those who were captured in the course of combat, they were kept as POWs in prison. Until it was possible to determine whether they could be charged with having committed war crimes, et cetera. We had to keep them in detention. We weren't going to let them open fire on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, those who were not released, while there were investigations that were conducted to determine whether crimes of war had been perpetrated, so there was an ongoing investigation. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who conducted or who was conducting this ongoing investigation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the security service bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the framework of the investigation carried out by the security service bodies, did the military prosecutor -- or did the military prosecutor have to be informed of the fact that there were people held in detention, and if he should have been informed of this fact, was he in fact informed?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was done. We had to forward reports from the security body of the 3rd Corps on POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, other witnesses have said that among these prisoners there were some who were exchanged. How can you explain the fact that there was an investigation into crimes of war and in spite of this fact, prisoners were exchanged? How would you explain this? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on that. That's what was done. But when criminal reports were filed against individuals or the Presidency would grant a sort of amnesty and then there was an exchange. But in the case of people against whom criminal reports hadn't been filed, well, these individuals would be used in exchanges of POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us something that we hear for the first time. It's line 7 in the transcript. You say that the Presidency should issue a document allowing the exchange to take place. Which Presidency are you referring to? War Presidency? Which Presidency are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I'm a hundred per cent sure. I'm not a lawyer. I'm a member of the military. But I think that the Presidency concerned is the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the Presidency at a political level?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And this had nothing to do with my authority. When such a document arrived, the orders it contained were obeyed, and the exchange commission carried the order out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as you are one of the most high-ranking officers present, and if I'm following you correctly, you say that when an exchange took place, it was possible to have such an exchange only if the Presidency had granted permission for such an exchange, and they had to indicate that among those who were going to be exchanged, there were no individuals who were suspected of having committed crimes of war. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that this concerned individuals against whom criminal reports had been filed, or individuals who had already been sentenced or were serving their sentence. To have an exchange, you need some kind of an amnesty. But in the case of POWs, this was the commissions for exchange in the 3rd Corps, in operations group, that became involved in these matters. I'm not sure, because I wasn't really involved in this. I carried out orders. I would be glad if I've managed to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's perfectly clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I have a few questions for you on a -- concerning a meeting you had with another witness we have had here before in this courtroom, some seven, eight months ago. The subject of that meeting has not been discussed yesterday and this afternoon, but it has to do, I think, or I guess, with a number of things you told us yesterday and today. And you are the only person to whom I can put these questions. Do you remember that in the month November 1993 you had a meeting at the JNA barracks with an older Croat gentleman?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I often saw Croatian citizens who had remained in Travnik. I would often receive them. You have to be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, this was a gentleman who had been, according to his story, kidnapped and remained in a camp somewhere in the neighbourhood of Travnik, and afterwards was released and was taken into the basement of the Travnik military barracks. You remember now who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly because there was a group of them who were released, Rajkovic, Fisic. But that's correct, they were taken to the barracks, and I think some of them were in the clinic in Travnik, and some of them were placed in the cellar, perhaps. But the situation was particular. We took them to the barracks to provide them with protection and to make sure that they didn't find themselves in the situation that they had already been in. Because we believed that the group who had done what they had done might try threaten their lives again. So that this was a measure that was purely preventive. They weren't treated as prisoners or detainees. So that was our intention. And that was the way that members of the 17th treated these individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because the person I'm speaking about is Mr. Fisic [realtime transcript read in error "Visic"] and you his mentioned name. That is the older man that stayed for a while in the Travnik barracks. I don't want to discuss whether he was there freely or for his own protection or whatever else, but I want to relate -- to put a few questions on a conversation between him and yourself as told by him in January of this year to the Trial Chamber. He has been here on the 13th -- 30th of January, and I'd like to quote some things he said. First on the page 2270, he describes you as being a very gentle and human person. And then he tells us -- well, he told us about a conversation he had with you. He told you the story about his being detained elsewhere, in other such, as he said, together with others. And he describes also your reaction to that story, and that's the matter I'm talking about now. He quotes you as saying the following thing: "I can't stand this any more." These are your words in the French original: "I can't stand the situation concerning certain unities here. I will clarify the matter or otherwise I will go." And then he says, he's quoting you as saying: "I will call the President Izetbegovic." And then he says: "That's what Mr. Cuskic has done, and Mr. Izetbegovic has come to Travnik while we were still in the basement of the barracks." That's -- I quote him now on page 2271, the original French text. Well, I have a few questions about this conversation between the two of you. The first, of course, is whether this is an exact reflection of what you said. Do you recognise the words or do you say "I said something else," or ...

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise my position and my attitude, and I think that on the whole, this is fairly accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My second question, then, will be the following: If you say to him "I'm going to call President Izetbegovic," have you indeed done this also?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I'm a member of the military. I follow the law. I didn't contact -- I didn't phone Mr. Izetbegovic. I think at the time General Alagic was the commander of the 3rd Corps, and I wanted this problem to be discussed at the highest level. I wanted President Izetbegovic to be informed of the problem, and I wanted this problem to be solved in the area. Because it was tarnishing the honest reputation. I don't know if this was the result of what Alagic did, but sometime in mid-November, and paragraphs it was on the 15th of November, Mr. Izetbegovic in fact was in Travnik and he visited the barracks in Travnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. But you have no way of knowing whether Izetbegovic was told the story by Alagic or by someone else?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. I know that General Alagic informed President Izetbegovic of this event, and he requested that the problem of the El Mujahed and the behaviour of the Mujahedin be solved. He requested that they be placed under control. He didn't only inform President Izetbegovic. Commander Alagic also addressed the superior command and made some suggestions. I think he did this in written and in oral form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And by talking about superior command, you mean probably the Command Staff in Sarajevo? Mr. Delic, I remember as being the ...

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said as commander of the operations group, while he was the commander in Travnik, he addressed the 3rd Corps commander. But as corps commander, I also know that he contacted or addressed Mr. Izetbegovic and made such requests. So he addressed Mr. Izetbegovic when he visited Zenica and when he visited Travnik. He didn't only contact Mr. Delic about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... aren't you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And do you know what answer the President Izetbegovic has given or was it not reported to you?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When hearing his story, you said: "I will clarify these things or otherwise I will go. I will call President Izetbegovic." Apparently you are so unhappy with the situation that you threaten to leave the forces. What made you so unhappy in this situation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shocked by the behaviour and by the fact that civilians were taken from their houses, innocent people, especially when I heard the story about the killing of Mr. Popovic in such a horrific, brutal manner. I think that is a normal human mind could not do such a thing. So I was shocked, as an ordinary human being. I don't know how to explain it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Were you, after having told this story to your superior, Alagic, in any way personally involved in the further developments of the situation?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, as a commander, I ensured protection, family encounters, visits, et cetera. But as for subsequent matters, they were not in the hands of my bodies, so not part of my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My last question on the matter is the following: Did you, by any chance, or in whatever way, hear about an investigation into the case, into what happened, by police or public prosecutors or whatever?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you a precise answer. I think that there was an investigation by the military security service, but I don't know for sure and I can't tell you about any details, at what level, which prosecution, was it the civilian police. Because military security organs are responsible for members of the army, whereas the civilian authorities are for civilians. So I can't give you a specific answer. But I do know that my security organs were not involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: On the other hand, yesterday, and today also, you said that you had testified in a case pending in a court in Bosnia against the person who might also have been involved in this event. So that's the background of my question.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the background. I said that, as a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I received a summons from the prosecutor's office, I testified, I told them what I knew, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But that apparently is not about this event, or is it?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is partly linked to it. I don't know to what extent it is of interest for this case. Mr. Jonathan Schmidt knows best. It has to do with my knowledge about Meqtauf and his possible role in this, and that is what I testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. I'll not pursue these questions. I have just one remark to make. I was referring to the Witness Ivo Fisic, with an F, who testified on the 30th of January, 2004. I quoted from the French transcript, especially page 2271. That's for the record. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 5.20. The best idea is to have the break now and then we will resume after the break with possible questions by the Prosecution and the Defence. So we will resume at about a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Prosecution for their questions, I think there was a translation problem, so I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect, twice since the beginning of these proceedings, I tried to assist the Trial Chamber in drawing attention to a translation problem, and particularly when Your Honours were asking questions. And the same problem occurred today. So I think that while you were asking questions, we should not be allowed to ask for the floor, because I feel very embarrassed if I'm not given the floor. But in this specific case, I wanted to ask Your Honours, when the document PT669 was discussed, I wish to indicate that the first sentence has been mistranslated. This document begins with the words "we know 11 persons," and the translation says "we have 11 persons." So I felt the error to be substantive, and I wished to draw attention of Your Honours to this error so that the interpreters could provide the Judges with a correct translation in time. Thank you for hearing me out. I'm talking about document P616. I apologise. I made a mistake. P616. I gave the document the wrong number. Thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no problem. If you note a translation problem, because stand up immediately. But I thought that you wanted to ask a question of substance. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just to add to what my colleague has said: When the witness was testifying, he said precisely what Ms. Residovic has just said. We know he said 11 persons, and this is reflected in the transcript when you were asking your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. The document says "we have" instead of "we know 11 persons." So you're quite right. I shall give the floor now to Mr. Mundis. I think he has some questions emanating from the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do have just a few questions for the witness. But before we do that, I would like to point out to the Chamber and, as I indicated to the Defence at the break, during the line of questioning that the Presiding Judge put to the witness concerning P616, we were -- or I directed that the original of that document be retrieved from the Evidence Unit. During the break I've shown this to the Defence. I would like to show this original document, P616, in Bosnian to the witness and put a few questions to him, with your leave. And I will certainly make this available for the Trial Chamber, and also I think it should be shown to the accused, because they haven't seen the original of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you now have before you the original of P616. Earlier you were shown photocopies of this document. I simply ask you to look at the original document, and in light of your earlier comments I would ask you now if there's anything you would like to clarify or to explain, having had the benefit of seeing the original, which includes some markings in blue that were not visible on the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously an original document, registered under this number. But I still stand by all the comments I made as a military man with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you clearly see on the document a stamp of a unit within the 3rd Corps? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. There's a stamp and a registration number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I believe you told us earlier that the person who signed the document, Mr. Adilovic, according to the document, was the assistant commander for religious and morale, religious affairs and morale.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that that is what he was. I just said that that is the title indicated in the signature. I know him as -- I don't know him as such. I know him as the imam in Travnik and the director of the Medresa in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's right, sir. And my he question in English was: According to the document, the signature block of the document indicates that he held that position within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade on or about the 27th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. That is what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it's also clear, sir, is it not, from the subject line that Mr. Adilovic is not ordering helicopter transport but is simply requesting such transport?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says. But he's asking for transport for persons he knows, 11 Arabs and Turks, persons he knows, not members of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. I would ask now that the document be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. In the French translation, we are told persons he knew. In your own language, the document in your language, does it say "we know" or "we have 11 persons"? How would you interpret the first line in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your own language, yes. What is clear in your language? Because there's a difference. These persons, they may have asked for a helicopter for persons he knew, this person knew, but if he says "we have," it is not quite the same thing. So I'm asking you: What do you read in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite agree with your explanation. It's sufficient to read this. There's no interpretation needed. I will read it in Bosnian slowly, and I would ask the interpreters, and I apologise to them for speaking quickly. And it says: "We know 11 persons - Arabs and Turks, who need to go to Igman. So we are asking you to allow helicopter transport for them in one or two flights, when it's on your way. We are not asking a special flight for this." And in addition to my previous comment, saying that it was not in appropriate military language, one can see that this is not a priority issue, that it's not a question of battle, but simply transport of persons he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for the clarification. Because the English translation says "we have." And this does not correspond to "we know."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any recollection or knowledge about events occurring on Igman on or about the 27th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have no further need for the witness to have that document. If it could be returned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have just one other question in terms of clarification, Witness, from an answer that you gave in response to a question from the Trial Chamber. This is on page 54, at line 20. You were discussing how you had delegated responsibility for the care and protection of persons detained in the basement of the former JNA barracks in Travnik. And according again to the English transcript, you immediate reference to delegating that responsibility to, and the English says "Colonel Salko, the assistant for morale." I would ask you, sir, if you could please give us that individual's full name that you were referring to, this Colonel Salko.

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I gave his full name. Colonel Salko Dedic, my assistant for moral guidance. And the reason why I designated him is that, in addition to the people who were normally responsible for this was, first of all, because he was married to a Croat and he had good relations with Pavo Nikolic in Travnik. So I wanted to have the proper information and proper care for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, answering a question from the President of the Trial Chamber about fighting at Karaula from the 6th of September until the beginning of November, you said that you saw some Mujahedin in a part of a village and that you participated with them in two combat operations. Tell me, please, General: In that period of time, in addition to those Mujahedin, did other units take part in the defence of those lines that did not belong to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian Defence Council, the HOS, H-O-S, or some other units that were ready to defend Jajce and the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony yesterday, I was more specific when talking about the defence of this area between Travnik and Jajce. So HVO units did take part in defending Jajce, as well as HOS, H-O-S, the Territorial Defence, and my own brigade, which was already called the 7th Brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Regarding this group of Mujahedin in Gradina, this is a small group of some 15 people. A lot of hullabaloo is made about them. They couldn't have any significant effect in the struggle. Perhaps psychologically it meant something for the people of the village. But I have some experiences in a battle later on, when they took part with us. However, in this period, until the fall of Jajce, the line was 136 kilometres, almost a circle. The HVO, the Territorial Defence, the HOS, and the Krajina units that were already called the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina took part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After those events and the battles at Karaula, do you know where that group of Mujahedin went, and did you come across them ever again?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. His Honour Judge Swart drew your attention to a part of your conversation with Mr. Fisic, which you basically confirmed. Tell me, please, General: When you told Mr. Fisic that you would make a request to General Alagic, did this confirm your position that the question of the Mujahedin could be resolved only at the highest political level?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must now convey my personal opinion. Perhaps 95 per cent of former JNA officers who held command positions, not only in my brigade but in brigades in the area of Travnik and under the 3rd Corps command, we simply were not convinced of the justification or necessity or correctness of the presence and actions of the Mujahedin. And the position of Commander Alagic and Commander Hadzihasanovic was that it should be resolved, and this could only be resolved by political institutions. It was our legal obligation to follow instructions received from the political level. So we knew that President Izetbegovic gave orders to General Delic, General Delic to General Hadzihasanovic, and so on. And we respected that command. That is how we were trained and that is what we did in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One further question. Well mentioned the Mujahedin at Karaula. Did you know at the time, in 1993 and later, that certain groups of Mujahedin were located in other areas around Teslic, around Konjic, sometimes smaller groups, in any way, parts of the country that had nothing to do with the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FIKRET CUSKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I did not know about that. We were under a communications blockade, totally surrounded for a year, so I only knew about the area in which the operations were conducted. The area of Zenica, Travnik, and nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General, your testimony is over. You answered questions put to you by the Defence, the Prosecution, and the Judges yesterday and today. We thank you for coming to testify in The Hague. We wish you a safe journey home, and best wishes in your future life.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I look forward to a good pension, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence tells us that we have a witness. We have another 50 minutes left. We can begin now and continue tomorrow because the witness is waiting. And then we will continue tomorrow. We can start him today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the documents that I should like to tender, should we do that tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless we can do that quickly -- yes, please, go ahead. We will save a few minutes that way. I give you the floor. No. He's already here, so we'll do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I wish to check that you're hearing in your own language the interpretation of my words. If that is so, just let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness for the Defence. Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, I need to know your exact identity. Can you give me your first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mesud Hadzialic. I was born on the 14th of February, 1956, in the Foca, in the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today I teach at the electrical engineering faculty for transport and communications at the university in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you have an occupation at the time? If so, which? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, I was in the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the beginning of 1992, I was still working in an institution called the maintenance institute of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which unit, and what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the Municipal Staff of Territorial Defence, and later I joined the communications battalion of the 3rd Corps. In the former army, Yugoslav People's Army, I had the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you previously testified in an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is it the first time for you to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before. This is the first time for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you be kind enough to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. We have 45 minutes before we adjourn. We'll be adjourning at 7:00 p.m. I'd like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed today and tomorrow. You'll first have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel. After their examination-in-chief, which will take up part of the hearing tomorrow, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will cross-examine you. The purpose of their cross-examination will be to verify how credible your testimony is and to clarify some of the answers that you provide to Defence counsel. After this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may re-examine you. Their questions should be related to the Prosecution's questions. Then the three Judges sitting before you will certainly have some questions for you. The Judges may ask you questions that might be completely different from the ones put to you by both parties, but they may also be related to the questions put to you by the parties. As a rule, we ask questions to clarify certain issues or to fill any gaps that we feel need to be filled. If you find that a question is complicated, do your best to answer it, because we don't have any written documents about your testimony, and it is what you say here that will inform us. The parties or the Judges might show you documents in the course of your examination. This may constitute part of the procedure. If your question is too complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. I would also like to point out that, as you have taken the solemn declaration, you should not give false testimony, since false testimony is an offence. It's an offence throughout the world, and it's an offence in this court as well. Secondly, but this shouldn't be applicable to you, if a witness believes that his answer might provide information that could be used to prosecute him, the witness may refuse to answer the question. But in such an exceptional case, the Trial Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question, but the witness is granted a form of immunity. This is a provision that should help us determine the truth. If you encounter any difficulties, please inform us of the fact. As a rule, we work for an hour and a half, then we have a break, a 25-minute break, and then we continue for another hour and a half. Now we only have about 40 minutes left, but I will now give the floor to the Defence counsel, who will start their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Professor Hadzialic.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge has just provided you with some important information, but there is something I would like to add. We speak the same language, and you might want to answer my questions immediately. But it is necessary for my questions and your answers to be interpreted, so that the Chamber can follow us, as well as my colleagues in the courtroom. I'd be grateful if you could make a brief pause after I put my question to you. I also briefly pause after your answer. And in this way, we will ensure that your testimony is of assistance to the Chamber. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Hadzialic, you said you are now a professor at the engineering faculty at the University of Sarajevo. Please tell me when and where you were educated.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I completed the electrical engineering faculty in Sarajevo in 1978. I then served in the army, and as I had a scholarship from the former JNA, I worked in the maintenance institute in Travnik. I became -- I finished my work there as the chief of investigations. I completed my postgraduate studies in the technical faculty in Sarajevo, the electrical engineering faculty in Sarajevo, and I defended my doctoral thesis there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said you served in the JNA. Did you then obtain a rank of any kind, or rather, as you said you were a major, when did you obtain this rank and how did you obtain this rank?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I obtained the rank of major in 1991, at the beginning of 1991. I obtained it by going to certain schools and by following certain seminars. As I had graduated from civilian faculties, I had to train in this way. So I went to certain schools that enabled me to have a higher rank, that enabled me to have the rank that I would have had had the situation been normal and had my professional career developed in a normal manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, you immediately started working in the repairs and maintenance institution in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as an assistant at the electrical engineering faculty for a few months before an order was issued on commencing work in the maintenance institute in Travnik, and I finished my professional career in that field in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the maintenance institute in Travnik was involved in?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: It was involved in the military sphere. It was a military institution. Its main task was to repair, or rather, maintain the communication system in the former JNA. It was to develop and produce certain systems and certain devices for training communications officers in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who governed the institute? Who was in charge of the institute of the military institution in the former Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Well, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence was in charge Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the institute. It was the technical administration department that was in charge of it. This department is in Belgrade or was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us where exactly the institute in Travnik was located?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: This institute, the repairs institute, was in the centre of Travnik. It's right next to a barracks, which is now the barracks of the Federation army, and there is only a fence separating these two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA, together with the Serbian forces, attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina, what sort of situation was your repairs and maintenance institute in? Did you withdraw with the JNA or did something else occur?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: During that period, we were quite well prepared. We had prepared with the Territorial Defence and we managed to organise the workers and the officers in the institute who intended to stay on managed to organise themselves. So we managed to establish full control over all the institute's resources, at a time that there was a unit of the former army in the neighbouring barracks, and they were there with the reserve forces, which were in fact infantry forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when exactly the JNA withdrew from the barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I know the dates. I don't know the days. But I'm sure that the withdrawal of the army from Travnik occurred after we had started -- after we had taken charge of the institute, or rather, after the administration recognised the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that was in the month of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just provided a partial answer to my next question. Who took over the administration of the maintenance institute in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Since at the time communications with centres, or rather, with the state organs in the BH, the ministry and the Presidency, weren't functioning very well, we sent reports on the situation in the institute, and they suggested that the War Presidency in Travnik should temporarily take charge of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time did the Travnik War Presidency take over the administration of the institute, and did it appoint a temporary administration for the institute?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The War Presidency in Travnik did take over the temporary administration of the institute, and I was appointed as the temporary director of the institute. But my colleague -- I was supposed to have a Croatian counterpart, a certain deputy for the administration of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, how long did you perform the duties of the director of the maintenance institute in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Well, this temporary regime of administering the institute went on until about the end of July 1992. That's when an administration staff was elected and a kind of administration committee for the maintenance institute in Travnik was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that period, did you still hold a position of any kind in the institute, and were you able to follow the work of the institute?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I remained as a member of this supervisory body, whose task was to help to efficiently run the resources that the maintenance institute in Travnik had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, at any point in time in 1992 did you join the armed forces; and if so, which armed forces did you join?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In April 1992, I reported to them. And I actually became part of the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Municipal Staff at the time? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I think it was Ribo Haso, who is a brigadier now. I think that was the period when he assumed the duties of commander of the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of duties did you have to perform in the Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Given my experience in the field of telecommunications, and in the field of military communications, my task was to provide assistance, or rather, we were supposed to establish a communications system for units which were part of the Municipal Staff and for units that were under the control of the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about the function of the maintenance institute before the war. Could you now tell us what the function of the maintenance institute was at the beginning and in the course of 1992, and what sort of resources did the institute have?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Well, I will try to first provide you with my answer to the second question. The institute had resources that had remained. These were communications -- this was communications equipment, various sorts of technology for various tactical purposes, and they also had some equipment, although it wasn't a complete system of equipment, they also had some equipment that was in the warehouses of the communications administration in Belgrade. The institute, as someone who was responsible for developing and producing complex communications centres, had a warehouse in its surroundings. So some equipment remained in the institute, and we regarded this equipment as military equipment that could be provided to Territorial Defence units for their use. The institute still maintain the still regime. They worked on repairing the equipment we had in the warehouse. So the quality of the equipment was at the required level. Naturally, the institute started dealing with certain technical problems, minor problems, that were encountered in the Territorial Defence with their equipment. The equipment was equipment that was obtained from radio amateurs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were the director of the maintenance institute, could you tell us whether this equipment was distributed, the equipment that the institute had was distributed; and if so, according to whose decision?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Well, during that period of time, the -- I was under a lot of pressure in the institute. I was under a lot of pressure from the HVO military structures. They wanted the available equipment in the institute to be redistributed. Since there were workers who were Bosniaks and Croats in the institute, the Territorial Defence and the HVO had information on the amount of equipment and on the state of the equipment. Since the HVO exerted pressure on a daily basis, the only way to preserve the status of the institute, the only way to ensure that it didn't fall into the hands of some military formations, was to act in accordance with the War Presidency decisions and to distribute the available equipment, or rather, the military devices, to HVO members and to members of the Territorial Defence in Travnik. We also did this in the case of Territorial Defence units which were outside the Travnik, if they had received authorisation for such equipment, for the use of such equipment, from the Travnik War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with that decision issued by the War Presidency, what was the principle followed when distributing the equipment you had and when sharing it among the Territorial Defence and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: The equipment was shared out on an equal basis. This was what was done whenever the Presidency signed an order. Perhaps the equipment wasn't identical, perhaps the systems weren't identical, but the agreement was that each side should receive the same amount of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the equipment was being distributed, did the War Presidency in your institute take into account how well equipped the HVO units and the Territorial Defence units were, or was this principle applied regardless of how these units were equipped?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Well, as an institute, we weren't able to find out how well HVO units were equipped. We knew how well the Territorial Defence units were equipped, though. In order to find a peaceful solution to this issue, we had to ensure that the equipment was distributed equally to both sides, that each side was given the same amount of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: How long did you remain in the Municipal Staff, and what duties did you assume afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I remained in the staff until the formation of the 3rd Corps, which is when I was assigned to communications battalion within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your main tasks in the communications battalion in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Since the corps covered a wide area and a number of units, it was necessary to become more engaged in training and engaging those units. My main task was to work together with the commanders in the communications battalion, to create the conditions for the system of command and control, or rather, to create the conditions that would ensure that the communication system was functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you equip units with communications equipment, and how did you equip 3rd Corps units with such equipment?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Well, we can't talk about equipping units and the command with the communication systems. These weren't complex systems that were used to establish a system of command and control. It was more a matter of individual devices for these purposes. The main source of such equipment was the equipment that had remained from the JNA. Units would obtain equipment from the warehouses of the institute on the basis of Presidency decision. Some of this equipment came from the Territorial Defence warehouse. But on the whole, this equipment was equipment such as amateur radio devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are an expert in the field of telecommunications. Tell me: What sort of staff did the command in the 3rd Corps have when its battalion -- when its communications battalion was formed?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: When the battalion -- when the communications battalion was formed, it consisted mostly of people who had served either in the former JNA and who had that sort of establishment, or it consisted of people who had some sort of experience in that field or had been involved in work as radio amateurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you were involved in training and in equipping units, tell me: Did you ever start training men in order to establish a communications system within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Given the variety of the equipment we had, given the difficult conditions, it was necessary to carry our tasks out, and the job that a communications officer has is very demanding, since such people have to be trained and have to be provided with the adequate knowledge, it was necessary to rapidly establish the relevant procedures and to provide them with the relevant technology. So individuals and units had to be trained to carry out this task. Because we believed that a lack of -- we believed that our lack of technology -- we could compensate for our lack of technology by providing men with better training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor: Which cadres did you train and where was the training carried out?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: These were mostly personnel that were assigned to communications units, or were going to be assigned to those units, and personnel who were to be assigned as commanders. We started with those personnel. And the training was provided in an organised fashion in Zenica, in premises assigned to the communications battalion, and in the barracks, and on the ground as well, wherever we had a chance of training people with the use of these devices. We devoted special attention at the beginning to the training of encoders, people who had to encode, encrypt documents, and also persons who would later be using such documents as operators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have just said how important it was to train people for the communications system, tell me: Does this system have any significance for the overall effect of the army, or rather, is it in connection with a system of command and control?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Allow me to use the NATO name, C-3, they refer to them, as command, control, and communications. Therefore, it is not possible to develop an efficient system of control and command without an effective communication system, and I mean both in terms of communications and in terms of the security of communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have just told us how important it was for the personnel to be properly trained, but for communications to be effective, what else is necessary?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: In addition to manpower, a very important element is the equipment, or rather, the integration and establishment of the functions of the equipment under given conditions. As the technologies were diverse, it required a lot of effort for them to become fully functional.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told me a moment ago which were the main sources of the equipment. Tell me now what kind of communications equipment the Territorial Defence had at its disposal, and later the ABiH army.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: I shall try and be brief and divide it into three different levels, according to the strategy in place. For the combat level, to ensure communications during combat operations, the equipment and number of devices was absolutely insufficient for the level of communication between units, that is, battalions and brigade commands. It was possible to establish such communications on an individual basis, which means you would need five channels, but you could make only one channel functional. And as for the operational level between brigade command, staff commands, and the 3rd Corps command, this was supported with equipment coming from radio amateur institutions and occasionally using the centres for observation and information. So, as I was saying, communications at the combat level hardly existed, with the exception of hand-held amateur radios, which cannot be used under those certain conditions. For the tactical level, the equipment of the former JNA was used, mostly conventional devices, and devices that could be maintained in Travnik, whereas for the third level, mainly radio amateur equipment was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in establishing this system in the 3rd Corps, did you have any priorities, or rather, did you focus on establishing one particular set of communications in relation to others, or could you briefly describe the ways in which you established the system in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: The available equipment dictated the priorities. Certain devices could not be used for combat level, could not be used for the tactical level. So what we had dictated the solutions. But at the command level, we did our best to ensure exchange of information between unit commands and the 3rd Corps command. I said that we tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In those days, what was the infrastructure like that you relied on in order to establish this priority level of communications between superior and subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: The concept of the former army, and any army in a particular territory, is to use to a maximum the resources of public communications systems or operators, as we call them today. In our case, we tried to use the resources of the postal system, a part of the system of the public post office, with wired infrastructure, and certain commutation that was located in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us: In addition to this basic infrastructure in the area of Travnik, were there any other elements that could establish communications, and did you use that infrastructure; and if you did not, why?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: Apart from these public resources, there were resources of the centres for information and observation. Such centres existed in all municipalities before the war. But our situation was such that we didn't use those resources, for the simple reason that the centres for information and observation were intended to monitor aircraft in the airspace above the municipality of Travnik, Novi Travnik, or Bugojno, for instance. So that at first we left those systems aside and let them be used for their primary purpose. We could have used the electricity supply systems, but they used a different frequency, so we didn't use them either. There were no other serious providers of communications in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in view of the situation, such as it was, in Travnik, and especially in view of the configuration of the ground, tell us: To what extent was it possible or difficult to use -- using this infrastructure to establish a communications system?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: The answer to this question was two parts to it. If we're talking about public resources, then these communications could be used quite well, using the cables of the postal service of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But because of constant squabblings and disputes over the use of those cables, these cables were frequently out of use. So they were not available. But for the organisation of the system of control and command, radio communications are much more important, and it should be said straight away that Travnik and its surroundings, that is, Mount Vlasic and the hills leading to Vlasic, and in the direction of Zenica, are difficult for radio communication. Because you have to use intermediaries, that is, features from which all the participants are visible, to make sure that you have proper communications, or to use free radio channels at the operative, tactical level, which are subject to disturbances and can be obstructed by features on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Establishing the communications system in the 3rd Corps, especially in the area of Travnik, did you come across other obstacles in 1993 which prevented you from establishing a stable and reliable system of communication between higher-level and lower-level commands?

utterances.speaker: MESUD HADZIALIC
utterances.text: This was a period when certain lines had already been established between the Serb side and the ABiH and the HVO, and those lines had to be secured mainly with wired systems, and to some extent with radio systems. In view of the location and the area that needed to be covered, we -- our main problem was the shortage of appropriate wire cables which are resilient to bad weather and which are laid above the ground. They were not available, and it was difficult to find them. Then there was the problem of power supply for such systems, in view of the fact that units were located in places where there was no electricity. And if there were electricity lines, they were cut; they were broken. There were no alternative sources of power or energy, and what I mean, various generators. Here and there, one could find a leftover military generator that was used for higher-level command. Then there was a shortage of batteries that were not maintained, and they couldn't be recharged because of the shortage of electricity. So that then there were failures, shortage of parts, as the equipment was being used under conditions that they were not adapted to. So these were very serious difficulties which we had to grapple with. For instance, we would have more than ten participants using the same wires, so that if somebody calls up on that line, he would hear all the other nine persons. So you would have to indicate by name who you wanted to talk to. So we did have a lot of difficulty, but we did our best to ensure conditions for the communication of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to interrupt your testimony. It is four minutes to 7.00. So, Professor, you will continue your testimony tomorrow. We're working in the afternoon. So it will begin at 2.15, so be present at that time. In the meantime, you are prohibited from meeting the parties. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you are now a witness of justice, not a witness of either party. So make the best of your time, but don't meet with anyone. I'm going to ask the usher to be kind enough to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of the afternoon tomorrow, at 2.15, I will give the floor to the Defence to tender exhibits into evidence. I will hear the observations of the Prosecution. If there is no dispute, we will ask the registrar to give the numbers to those exhibits. If there is a dispute, we will deal with them in due course. At the end of that stage, I will give the floor tomorrow to the Prosecution, who are going to orally respond to the oral motion that you formulated. We have asked the Prosecution to respond before this evening, but in any event, it will be tomorrow. I gather that the Prosecution will need some 20 minutes to respond to this question and to tell us the origin of the documents received. After that, we will have the witness brought back into the courtroom and we will continue with his testimony. If there are no other questions to be addressed, I'm going to adjourn the meeting, and I invite you to come back tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of November, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.
